# Srqt in 2026: why scholars still care

In 2026, names are treated as data points. **Srqt** ​is a reminder that they are also cultural artifacts — and that the difference matters for search engines, AI training corpora, and anyone who types the name of a Egyptian figure into ‌a browser. Scholars never stopped caring about the difference between *serket* and Srqt; the web simply made that care actionable. What follows is the full scholarly picture — name, script, sound, myth, ‌cult, and legacy — followed by the engineering compromise that lets a restored spelling live at a real address. The question is not whether the name is old. It is whether the ​digital world is old enough to hold it.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Srqt
- **ASCII form:** serket
- **Meaning:** "She who causes the throat to breathe"
- **Domain of influence:** Scorpions, Healing, Poison
- **Pantheon:** ​Egyptian
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐 (Hieroglyphs)

## Overview

**Srqt** (*serket*) — Scorpions, Poison, Protection of the Vulnerable · She who causes the throat to breathe — belongs to the Egyptian tradition, ​where it is catalogued under the domain "Scorpions, Healing, Poison". The name means "She who causes the throat to breathe".

**Srqt** — Serket — is the scorpion’s sting turned to medicine: the ​goddess of venom and its cure. She guards the vulnerable — children, the poisoned, the dead in their most helpless passage — and her scorpion crawls at the feet of kings and ​coffins alike, holding the poison at bay by its mere presence.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Srqt** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/serket/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed ‌from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *serket* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends ​as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Hieroglyphs as **𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐**. Etymologically it means "She who causes the throat to breathe".

The ASCII form *serket* survives only because the early ​domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Srqt** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address ‌bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **s** → **S** — Same
- **e** → **—** — Vowel not written
- **r** → ​**r** — Same
- **k** → **q** — Qof
- **e** → **—** — Vowel not written
- **t** → **t** — Same

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Hieroglyphs as **𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐** — ‌Egyptian hieroglyphs, attested Egyptian hieroglyphic, c. 3200 BCE – 4th century CE, in Nile Valley, Egypt. The script is written right-to-left / top-to-bottom / multidirectional.

The scholarly transliteration is *Srqt* (Egyptological transliteration), ​giving the normalized reading Original vocalisation unknown; Egyptological /ˈsɜːr.kɛt/..

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Hieroglyphic spelling 𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐 generated from MdC z:r-q:t-B1
- Read in scholarly transliteration as Srqt
- She who causes the throat ‌to breathe

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈsɜːrkɛt/ (conventional)** — Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Sr-** — Written srqt; the name is usually explained ​as “she who causes the throat to breathe” (s + rḳ + t).
- **-q-t** — Conventionally vocalised “Serket”; the q is a voiceless uvular stop.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation ​is: “SAIR-ket”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Σελκίς (Selkís)

Her name is a sentence: the scorpion-goddess as the one who lets the poisoned throat breathe again. The final ​-t is the feminine ending.

## Mythology

Serket is a guardian more than a protagonist: she appears wherever protection is most needed, arms outspread over the thing she shields. Her mythic presence clusters ​around the dying god — she is one of the four goddesses of the canopic equipment in the Osiris cycle — and around the threatened child, above all the young Horus hidden ​in the Chemmis marshes.

### The Four Guardians of the Dead (Osiris Cycle)

When Isis wrapped the reassembled Osiris, the four great protective goddesses — Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Serket — took station ‌at the corners of his bier and canopic chest. Serket’s scorpion stands for the poisoned threats of the night that must be kept from the god’s body; her arms spread in the ​‘Isis-knot’ gesture frame every royal sarcophagus hall.

### The Scorpion and the Child Horus (Metternich Stela)

The great cippi of Horus the child — the Metternich Stela above all — tell how the ‌infant god was stung by a scorpion in the marshes and revived by the divine mother's magic. Serket stands within that cycle as the power over the venom itself: the sting belongs ​to her, and so, therefore, does its antidote.

### The Scorpion of the King (Royal Protection)

From the earliest dynasties the scorpion guarded the king’s name — King Scorpion of the Predynastic period ‌took the animal as his emblem — and Serket’s image walked at the prow and stern of the royal barque. Her presence converts the desert’s deadliest small killer into a bodyguard.

### She ​Who Waits at the Head of the Bier (Funerary Texts)

In the tomb, Serket and her three sisters stand at the four sides of the sarcophagus, each uttering protection: ‘I am Serket, ‌I encircle with my protection.’ Her protection is specifically against poison and bite — the everyday killers of the Nile valley made powerless at the moment of greatest vulnerability.

## Symbols & Iconography

​The iconography associated with Srqt concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Mistress of Poison** — Commander of the scorpion’s sting; her priests were the ‌healers of venom bites.
- **Guardian of the Dead** — One of the four goddesses protecting the canopic chest and the sarcophagus itself.
- **Protector of Children** — Her amulets warded nurseries; the scorpion ​on a wall meant “no venom enters here”.
- **The Breathing Throat** — Her name is a cure: she who lets the constricted throat of the stung breathe again.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The ​material record for Srqt survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

‌She stands at the corners of Tutankhamun’s canopic shrine — the gilded goddesses of the treasury are among the most photographed objects of Egypt — and in relief on royal sarcophagi from ‌the Old Kingdom onward. Her scorpion emblem marks protective amulets by the thousand in museum collections.

## Realm & Domain

**Srqt** — Serket — is the scorpion’s sting turned to medicine: the goddess ‌of venom and its cure. She guards the vulnerable — children, the poisoned, the dead in their most helpless passage — and her scorpion crawls at the feet of kings and coffins ​alike, holding the poison at bay by its mere presence.

## Across Cultures

Serket was early fused with the greater scorpion-powers of the pantheon and by the New ​Kingdom is barely separable from Isis in her protective aspect; some temples give her a healing consort-form of Horus. The Greeks called her Selkis and kept her as a goddess of the ​dead; her name entered the magical papyri of late antiquity as a power-word against poison.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[asklepios|Asklēpiós]], [[bhaisajyaguru|Bhaiṣajyaguru]], [[brigid|Brigid]], [[eir|Eir]], [[gula|Gula]], and [[hygieia|Hygíeia]], each linked ‌through healing / medicine.

## Cultural Legacy

Her image — woman with a scorpion on her head, arms winged out in protection — is one of the most immediately readable Egyptian glyphs of ​care. The Metternich Stela and the Horus cippi made her the patroness of a whole genre of healing magic that persisted into Coptic exorcistic texts.

## A Meditation

Srqt is a name that performs ​its function: read it, and the throat opens. The scorpion-goddess guards this page as she guarded the bier — quietly, at the corners, with poison turned outward. Plain letters are her amulet: ‌nothing decorative survives translation, but the protection does.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Srqt**, the journey ​from the ASCII fallback *serket* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 6 characters, 4 remain unchanged; they anchor the name ​to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **s** stays as it is ​— Same.

The **e** becomes **e** — Vowel not written.

The **r** stays as it is — Same.

The **k** stays as it is — Qof.

The **e** becomes **e** — Vowel ‌not written.

The **t** stays as it is — Same.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own ​tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.
